title: Out of nothing
hook: creation out of nothing: the world isn't God and isn't an accident, but a gift

segments.voice: Yesterday, perichoresis: Father, Son and Spirit dwelling in one another, a ring held open. Your line was god is a dance. Where did you make room for someone? Day one thousand seventy-three.

A potter needs clay. A carpenter needs wood. A cook needs at least an egg. The makers we meet start with something already there, and shape it. So here's a strange question, and Christians have asked it: when God made the world, what was the clay? The first line of the Bible doesn't stop to say. It simply begins: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." No workshop, no pile of material, no rival standing by. Christian teaching came to answer the clay question with three words, and those three words say something about the cup on your table and the hand holding it. Today: out of nothing.

Out of nothing. In Latin, ex nihilo. The teaching is that God didn't shape the world from something that was already lying around. Before creation there was God, and nothing else. The letter to the Hebrews puts it this way, in the King James: "the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that things which are seen were not made of things which do appear." Paul, in Romans, describes God as one who "calleth those things which be not as though they were." A voice, and then a world. Christian teachers draw two lines from this, one on each side. First line: the world is not God. It isn't a piece of God broken off, or God's body. A tree is a tree, a river is a river; they're made, and God is the maker. Second line: the world is not an accident. Nothing forced God's hand. There was no raw stuff that had to be used up, no rival who had to be beaten. So why make anything at all? The book of Revelation has the elders before the throne sing: "thou hast created all things, and for thy pleasure they are and were created." Some Christian writers read that pleasure as love: a world made because love likes to share. Between those two lines sits a third word: gift. If the world isn't God, it can be studied, used, cared for. If it isn't an accident, it was meant. Something meant, and handed over, is a gift. That turns an ordinary object into a quiet question. Not just, what is this for? But, who gave this?

Here's the practice: hold something and call it a gift. Pick up whatever is closest. A mug, a pen, an apple, a spoon, your own hand. Hold it for the whole sit. Feel its weight. Look at it as if you'd never seen it. Then trace it backward: who made it, what it's made of, where that came from, and keep going back as far as you can. Somewhere back there, the chain runs out of answers. Stay there a moment. If you pray, you can give thanks for it by name. If you don't, just say quietly: this was given. The bell holds the time.
Out of nothing. The teaching that God made the world from no material at all: not God, not an accident, but a gift.
Your line: from nothing, for love. Today, before you throw one thing away, hold it for a second and ask who gave it. Day one thousand seventy-three.

howItsDone: Christians confess God as maker in the creeds, which begin with God the Father, maker of heaven and earth, and some give thanks before meals or at the start of the day for what they receive.

original.note: Hebrew: created. The verb in the Bible's first line: God created the heaven and the earth.

trapdoor: what you thought: out of nothing is a riddle about the big bang.
what it means: God made the world from no material at all, so the world isn't God and isn't an accident: it's a gift.
what a scholar hears: Hebrews 11:3 and Romans 4:17, the texts teachers lean on, since Genesis 1:1 itself doesn't stop to say what God used.

notes: Reading God's 'pleasure' in Revelation 4:11 as love is attributed to 'some Christian writers', not stated as the text's meaning. Confirm.

Some scholars read Genesis 1:1–2 as God ordering a formless deep rather than making from nothing; the script avoids claiming Genesis 1:1 itself teaches creation out of nothing and leans on Hebrews 11:3 and Romans 4:17. Confirm the framing is fair.
2 Maccabees 7:28 (God made them of things that were not) is often cited for this teaching; left out because it is not in every Christian Bible on this broad path.
Original: בָּרָא (bara), 'created', from Genesis 1:1. The common claim that only God is the subject of bara is left out under the claims rule.
